h: The politics of prevention: choking protest before it begins
dek: Writing in The News Minute, lawyer and public law researcher Sithara Sarangan argues that arrests on an aircraft, internet shutdowns, locked metro stations and the denotification of Jantar Mantar are together quietly ending the right to protest.
body: The writer's basic point is that when a protest is stopped before it begins, the government gains the most: no crowd gathers, no pictures are made, and all that is left is an official statement that order was kept. On 10 October Cockroach Janata Party members Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained inside the aircraft as soon as they landed in Delhi, while the Jantar Mantar protest was yet to happen.

She recalls that in 2018 the Supreme Court said clearly that protest can be regulated, but cannot be ended just because it causes the administration trouble. So removing Jantar Mantar and suggesting Ramlila Maidan, Burari and the CBD Ground is no proof that the right is being protected. How easy a place is to reach, and what the conditions for permission are, decide whether this is an arrangement or a hidden ban.

The article puts the internet shutdown in the same chain. From 10 pm on 9 October, mobile internet was cut for 24 hours within four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing. The writer does not call this illegal in itself, but she recalls the test set in the Anuradha Bhasin judgment, and notes that the shutdown also hurts shopkeepers, people who depend on digital payments, and journalists recording police action.

On 9 October the Supreme Court had found the curbs on metro and rail excessive. Even so, a contempt petition alleges that some stations stayed closed, and on 12 October movement was stopped at six stations. The writer argues that these steps must be weighed not one by one but by their total burden, because together they suppress gathering, speech and scrutiny, all three.

She sees the biggest danger in all this becoming normal. After the preventive detention of thousands, it is hard to avoid a phrase like 'undeclared Emergency', though this is not the declared Emergency of 1975. Citing Anne Applebaum, she warns that democracy can be hollowed out by elected governments too, and the real test is whether order makes freedom possible or becomes an excuse to lock it up.
nazar: This piece is written in the language of law, not slogans, and that is why it stings more. The government can justify each restriction on its own, but when airport arrests, internet shutdowns, locked metro stations and the loss of a protest site all come together, only one picture emerges: power wants to clear away those who ask questions before it has to hear the questions.

The court said twice that services should not be shut, and still the stations stayed closed. If even court orders do not reach the ground, what does a citizen have left but the street, and now even the street is being taken away.
sawal: Who will ask for proof of stopping a protest that never happened?
ref: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan judgment (2018)
The Supreme Court said there cannot be a total ban on protest at Jantar Mantar and the Boat Club. Protest can be regulated, not ended.
Anuradha Bhasin judgment (2020)
The Supreme Court ruling on the Kashmir internet shutdown: speech on the internet is constitutionally protected, and shutdown orders must be proportionate and made public.
ank: Mobile internet shut within a four-kilometre radius

h: Neha Bora's anger: when fear breaks, it comes to the street
dek: In The News Minute, Nidhi Suresh uses AISA president Neha Bora's story to ask why women and queer people are at the front of this movement, and why their anger is not 'hysteria'.
body: The article opens with a scene: a detention bus stopped by protesters, and Neha Bora jumping out of it, in a video that spread within minutes. The writer argues that anger has now moved out of private corners into streets, screens and homes, and it is not male. Neha Bora, who uses 'they/them' pronouns, is its face.

The writer met them on 11 October at a detention centre on the outskirts of Delhi. Since 2 October AISA has been calling protests against the Special Intensive Revision of the voter rolls and for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. According to the article, Neha was detained more than ten times in two weeks, sometimes twice a day, and they call detention their 'rest hours'. During the NEET protests in July they were on a 23-day hunger strike at Jantar Mantar.

Neha says that helplessness and fear, once thought to be ordinary people's set response to power, have now broken. The writer adds that political anger is accepted as legitimate only when it comes from a man; the rest is brushed off as hysteria. She mentions seeing injuries at the detention centre and hearing communal and casteist abuse.

Asked about the risk, Neha points to the rape cases of Hathras, Unnao and Delhi and to the lynching of Muslims, and says that crores of Indians do not even have the option to protest. The article also shows that this anger is organised: every morning some activists go out to check barricade points, stay in touch with journalists and run a large social media team.

The writer accepts that Neha's tiredness is real. They long for rest and for clothes that are not torn, but they cannot stop. The conclusion is that, unlike sadness, despair or fear, anger keeps a person going and gives courage, and in Neha's words it feels like justice.
nazar: The history of movements is full of male heroes, and women's anger in them has often been turned into a footnote. The most lasting pictures of this movement may well be of those who climbed the barricades, were dragged away and came back again. That is the real challenge for the government: the breaking of fear is a far bigger event than any one resignation.
sawal: Since when has a woman's anger been counted as politics?
ref: AISA
All India Students' Association, a student body linked to the CPI (ML) Liberation. It has a strong presence in JNU and Delhi University.

h: From tea to slippers: satire and daring return to the language of protest
dek: Frontline political editor Anand Mishra looks at how the movement against Gyanesh Kumar has changed the idiom of protest with slogans, memes and slippers.
body: Anand Mishra's column is less about the movement's demands and more about its language. After student sit-ins over paper leaks and job scams, it is now the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter rolls and the conduct of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar that are troubling the ruling party, and the writer hears a new ring in the style of protest on the streets and on social media.

He gives the example of Bengaluru, where the Cockroach Janata Party held a slipper protest at Freedom Park on 8 October after a people's tribunal on the SIR. Slippers were waved from the stage and women were told to make them a weapon against those who oppress them. A post by CJP's Saurav Das called Gyanesh Kumar 'Gyanu' and warned him that the cockroaches are coming.

The column also includes a viral video from the INDIA bloc protest in Delhi, in which Priyanka Gandhi and Supriya Shrinate are seen singing. The most popular slogans, the writer says, came from the protest by Delhi University women students demanding safe public spaces after the gang rape of a minor in September. Music videos, dances and memes were made on them.

The writer recalls that during the 36-day youth movement in July, the ruling party was enraged by the use of swear words, and an FIR was filed against a young woman. He then lists the long tradition of symbolic protest inside Parliament: from Atal Bihari Vajpayee's bullock cart in 1973 to masks and mimicry.

Recalling Krishan Chander's Ek Gadhe ki Aatmakatha (Autobiography of a Donkey) and the satire of Shrilal Shukla, the column ends by asking whether Indians are rediscovering their lost humour. The writer says it is better to spread laughter than rumours.
nazar: Satire has always been the weapon of the weak, and it is also what stings power the most. When mocking ministers brings an FIR and cartoonists face censorship, slippers and memes are not just clowning; they are a stubborn insistence on speaking. The movement's real strength may be that it has turned fear into laughter.
sawal: Why is power so afraid of laughter?
ref: Cockroach Janata Party
A youth platform that began as satire in 2026 and grew into a movement after the NEET paper leak. Its founder is Abhijeet Dipke.
Ek Gadhe ki Aatmakatha
Krishan Chander's satirical novel that strikes at the bureaucracy and politics of independent India through the eyes of a donkey.

h: Ajay Bokil: the tandav has begun, but no one knows the way
dek: In an Amar Ujala blog, Ajay Bokil asks where the opposition's movement actually wants to go, when the constitutional ladder to remove Gyanesh Kumar is so high.
body: The writer begins with Rahul Gandhi's remark calling this movement Shiva's tandav (the cosmic dance of destruction). In his view it is an opposition-led movement in which the public takes part only indirectly, and it is hard to say yet whether it will create something new or cool down.

Much of the article is legal arithmetic. The Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge: a motion by 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha MPs, then a three-member inquiry committee, and finally a special majority in both Houses. According to the writer, neither the government nor the opposition has these numbers, and the Supreme Court can criticise but cannot remove.

The writer believes the opposition has partly succeeded in building a narrative: that the government is surrounded by allegations, elections are being rigged and the people's voice goes unheard. Young people's anger over paper leaks, entrance exam irregularities and vote theft, all three, is visible on the streets, and videos from Delhi have spread around the world.

He sees two narratives facing each other: in one, the dictatorship of Modi and Shah and a crackdown on women and journalists; in the other, the whole thing is called an anti-Modi toolkit and a plot to destabilise. The writer also notes that the INDIA bloc and the CJP are holding separate marches for the same demand.

His conclusion is that Rahul Gandhi names the Prime Minister as the real target but offers no roadmap. The opposition wants to keep the issue alive until the next Lok Sabha election, and the BJP wants the demand for resignation to drag on so that other issues fade. Gyanesh Kumar has two and a quarter years left, and the writer quips that perhaps he wants to set some record like T.N. Seshan.
nazar: Bokil's constitutional arithmetic is correct, but that same arithmetic is the reason for the movement: when the road to removal is almost closed and the government has a majority in appointments, what is left but the street to demand accountability? Giving space in the article to voices claiming a foreign 'Islamist-Left' plot only fans the same toolkit narrative that the writer himself calls one side of the story.
sawal: If the road to removal is closed, where do we demand accountability?
ref: Impeachment-like process
The Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only by a special majority of both Houses of Parliament, on proven misbehaviour or incapacity.
T.N. Seshan
Chief Election Commissioner from 1990 to 1996, who enforced the model code of conduct strictly and raised both the Commission's power and its standing.

h: Sachin Sharma: the real test of the movement is the ballot box, not the street
dek: In an ETV Bharat article, Sachin Sharma asks why the real test of the protest on Delhi's streets is the election, not the courts or the media.
body: The writer sums up five days of the movement in three strands: the Cockroach Janata Party's sit-in that began on 10 October, AISA president Neha Bora's flash protests around Connaught Place and the Parliament area from 10 to 13 October, and the Congress march to the Supreme Court on 12 October, which he says was the biggest.

In his view the government was harshest on the CJP. Embarrassed by the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan after the NEET paper leak movement in July, the government did not want to take any risk this time. Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained on arrival, and Das and Ranka were sent to Tihar for five days after raising slogans again. The writer claims the Home Ministry was relatively soft on the Congress.

The article links Neha Bora's rise to the absence of the CJP leaders. Rahul Gandhi kept them on stage at his press conference, which fuelled speculation that, like Kanhaiya Kumar, they might join the Congress. According to the writer, the Congress does not even name the CJP and sees it as a B-team of the Aam Aadmi Party. The petition filed in the Supreme Court had a dozen errors, and notice was issued only after they were corrected.

The writer also notes that in the festive season shopkeepers from Khan Market to Connaught Place were starved of customers, and metro and traffic were limited. In place of Jantar Mantar, Ramlila Maidan, Burari and the CBD Ground in Shahdara were suggested. They are far from Parliament and their rent runs from thousands to lakhs of rupees a day.

In the end the writer makes election results the test. In recent by-elections the BJP-NDA won four of five Assembly seats and one Lok Sabha seat, and the BJP took 38 of 44 seats in the Gandhinagar Municipal Corporation. His conclusion is that the opposition looks weak for now, and only the 2027 elections in five states will show how seriously the people took its case.
nazar: This piece looks at the movement with a cold, almost official eye, and that is why it is worth reading: it shows the yardstick that analysis sitting close to power uses. But the question of democracy is not just a count of by-elections. Those whose names were cut from the voter rolls are not even part of that count, and that is the real complaint of this movement.
sawal: How will people whose names were struck off change the results?
ref: NEET paper leak movement
A 36-day student movement at Jantar Mantar in July 2026, led by the CJP. According to the writer, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned after it.

h: Grok and Gemini caught calling real photos fake
dek: A BOOM investigation: AI chatbots called two real photos of police action old and from somewhere else, and that answer went around social media as proof.
body: As soon as photos of the protests against the Election Commission spread, many people began posting screenshots of AI chatbot answers to dismiss them. BOOM checked two such photos and found that both were real and recent, while the chatbots' claims were wrong.

The first photo is from Mumbai and shows a woman with a child in detention. She was among the parents who had come with about 300 Adivasi (indigenous) students who walked from Nashik to Mumbai against the poor state of Adivasi schools and hostels. Gemini said it was from a 2024 anganwadi (childcare workers') protest. BOOM found it was a photo taken by Hindustan Times photographer Raju Shinde on 7 October 2026. NDTV had run a fact-check video based on the same wrong Gemini answer, which was later taken down.

The second photo shows a policeman in Delhi gripping a Sikh man by the throat. Grok said it was from a 2020 protest in Kolkata. According to BOOM, it was taken by Saumya Khandelwal for The New York Times on 11 October 2026. Even when BOOM asked, Grok repeated the same wrong answer, and the sources it cited had nothing to do with the photo.
BOOM says that using chatbots to fact-check recent events risks spreading lies even further.
nazar: Now no one even has to invent a lie to deny police excess; one wrong answer from a machine is enough. When big channels also trust it, the small organisations that check facts matter even more.
sawal: Has a machine's answer now become bigger than an eyewitness?
ref: Reverse image search
A way to find the earliest publication and source of a photo by putting it into a search engine.

h: She showed her press card and was still shoved into the bus
dek: A Newslaundry journalist writes about what happened to her in detention while covering the protest against the Election Commission in Delhi.
body: In this account in Newslaundry's 'First Person' section, the journalist writes that around 11.15 on Saturday morning she and her colleague Ashwini Kumar Singh had just left after recording video at the Jantar Mantar protests when news came that two more colleagues had been detained near New Delhi railway station.

When they got there, the police pushed and dragged Ashwini, snatched his phone and abused him. When the writer stepped in, she too was pulled into the bus. Showing her press card made no difference. She alleges that a man standing behind her in the bus touched her inappropriately, and moved forward when she objected. She asks what arrangements there were for the safety of the women detained.

According to the report, about 30 journalists have been detained since 10 October, some despite Supreme Court directions. That same day a CRPF jawan told her he would never raise a baton against an unarmed person, which the writer calls the only human moment of the day. After a headcount at Chhatrasal Stadium she was taken to Adarsh Nagar police station, where the station officer said it was for her 'safety'.
After her release, a bus driver on the Safdarjung flyover offered protesters a free ride.
nazar: Stopping a journalist from doing her work, shoving her into a bus with the crowd and then calling it 'safety' is a direct attack on press freedom. The detention of thirty journalists should be seen not as separate incidents but as a pattern.
sawal: When journalists themselves are detained, who will show the truth?
ref: First Person
A journalist's personal account based on their own experience, in which they are themselves a witness to the event.

h: Ashok Bhatia: a stubborn demand for resignation, the opposition's need or a test for an institution?
dek: In Prabhasakshi, Ashok Bhatia argues that the question of the Election Commission's credibility is real, but that Gyanesh Kumar's resignation is also a political story the Congress needs.
body: The writer begins with the opposition. The INDIA alliance is often pulled apart over ideology and seats, so it was looking for an issue that would unite everyone and touch people's feelings. In his view, the row over Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar has become that issue. It has now moved from the street to the Supreme Court.

He traces the dispute to an Indian Express report which says the two election commissioners recorded written objections about 14 times in ten months. The opposition alleges that the chief commissioner sidelined them. Along with this, according to the article, about 13.30 crore names were removed in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists across 30 states and union territories. The Commission calls it a clean-up of fake and duplicate names; the opposition calls it vote theft.

Bhatia argues that the Congress's insistence on resignation is not only about principle. It is also about lifting workers' morale after election defeats, putting those defeats down to faults in the machinery, and keeping its central place in the alliance. Rahul Gandhi is also targeting the section of the 2023 law that gives commissioners immunity from legal action.

On the other side, the BJP calls it desperation born of the fear of defeat and says that differences inside a multi-member body are a sign of a healthy democracy. The writer points out that removing a chief election commissioner is as hard as removing a Supreme Court judge, and almost impossible with the present numbers. So, in his view, the opposition's real aim is to put the government on trial in the court of the people.

In the end he says that democracy runs not on arithmetic but on the fairness of institutions and on trust. If a haze hangs over the voter list before every election, trust will fall. His advice is that the matter be decided not on the street but in the Supreme Court, on the basis of evidence.
nazar: This piece does not back the movement, yet it carries an admission: the crisis of the Commission's credibility is real, and the point about the 14 objections cannot be brushed aside as opposition propaganda. It is worth reading because even in places seen as close to the government, the debate has now shifted from 'the charges are false' to 'let the court decide'.

But the advice of 'the court, not the street' is only half the story. The lakhs of people whose names were cut have neither lawyers nor time. Taking to the street is often the only way for a voice to reach the court, and the fear of jail for waving the Tricolour narrows that road further.
sawal: If the evidence is in court, why the guard on the street?
ref: Article 324(5)
The constitutional provision under which a chief election commissioner can be removed only in the way a Supreme Court judge is, by a special majority in both Houses of Parliament.
Prabhasakshi
A Hindi news and opinion website. This piece appeared in its politics analysis section as the writer's personal view.

h: Ateeq Jarallah: the battle for Bab al-Mandab in Yemen at a turning point
dek: In Al Jazeera, Ateeq Jarallah argues that the war on Yemen's western coast is tied to the Iran war, and its outcome will decide whether it becomes a new beginning or a long, draining fight.
body: Yemen's war has once again narrowed around the world's most sensitive sea route, the Bab al-Mandab strait. According to the writer, in the government-led 'Operation Yemen's Dawn', government forces have advanced towards the strait, and fighting with Houthi positions continues around Dhubab district and Dhubab airport.

Jarallah asks us to tell apart three things: retaking positions on the coast, holding them, and making the strait permanently safe. He says that even after the coast is taken, the Houthis can fire missiles and drones from other places and target ships in the Red Sea.

According to the writer, Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Presidential Leadership Council, now talks not just of stopping the Houthis but of liberating Sanaa. But that needs one command, reliable supplies and coordination. Differences over the question of the south will have to be managed, and since the southern Giants Brigades have played the most effective role in the coastal fighting, unity becomes even more necessary.

On the regional side, the writer says plainly that Houthi aggression cannot be separated from the Iran war. Citing a Reuters report, he claims that Iran's Revolutionary Guards were directing the Houthis' coastal activity and pushing them to raise tensions against Saudi Arabia. After deadly attacks on airports, a Saudi response is almost certain. Pakistan and Turkey have announced they will stand with Saudi Arabia under the 'Mecca Agreement', but the terms of their involvement are not clear.

In conclusion Jarallah sees two paths. If government forces hold the positions, the military and political balance could shift, even if the threat at sea does not end. If the advance stalls, there will be a long, draining war whose human and economic cost the whole region will pay. No settlement will last without power-sharing, mutual guarantees and maritime security.
nazar: This piece sees Yemen only as a military map, while its ordinary people have suffered hunger, disease and displacement for years. Between the Iran war, the Saudi alliance and the American election, Yemen is again becoming an arena for big powers. For India too this is not far away: disruption at Bab al-Mandab and Hormuz means costlier oil and insecurity for the lakhs of Indians working in the Gulf. The real question is when the negotiating table will be set, not who wins the next front.
sawal: Will victory at Bab al-Mandab bring peace to Yemen?
ref: Bab al-Mandab
The narrow sea passage linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. A large share of Asia-Europe trade and oil passes through it.
Mecca Agreement
A recent defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, under which an attack on one is treated as an attack on all.

h: Munzoul Assal: turning down a chance for dialogue in Sudan will cost dearly
dek: In Al Jazeera, researcher Munzoul Assal writes that doubts about a national dialogue initiative launched from army-held territory are fair, but rejecting it on day one would be wrong.
body: The war between Sudan's army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has gone on for more than three years. Munzoul Assal, a senior researcher at Norway's Chr. Michelsen Institute, believes that military victory alone will neither rebuild the country nor bring a divided society together. So every attempt at dialogue among Sudanese should be taken seriously.

The writer explains that in August a self-declared committee of 19 well-known figures was formed, chaired by Gasim Badri, president of Ahfad University. The committee met army chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and asked for legal restrictions on opposition leaders to be lifted. A decree followed, which speaks of dropping political cases against Sudanese living abroad who return for dialogue and giving them temporary legal protection. Assal sees this as a small but important step to build trust.

The civilian coalition 'Sumoud', led by former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, and the 'Tasis' coalition, which includes the RSF, have rejected the initiative. They fear that dialogue in army-held areas will give Burhan legitimacy. The writer finds these worries fair: the committee is not elected, it began in Khartoum, and if it looks too close to the army it will be seen as part of Burhan's agenda.

Even so, Assal argues that preparing for dialogue cannot wait for the war to stop. A ceasefire and getting aid through are essential, but these can go on side by side. The committee's real test will be whether it can include anti-army forces, displaced people and those living outside army areas without fear.

The writer's conclusion is that this initiative should be seen neither with too much hope nor with blind suspicion. If the committee can build an independent and inclusive process, those rejecting it should rethink their decision.
nazar: Sudan today is among the world's biggest humanitarian crises, yet it is almost missing from the news. The most important point of the piece is that peace will begin not at the table of the men with guns but with the participation of ordinary Sudanese. But it is also true that trust is hard to build in a process that lies in the shadow of one military side. If the voices of people driven from home in their own land do not reach this dialogue, it too will remain just another initiative on paper.
sawal: Can a dialogue begun in the army's shadow win trust?
ref: Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
Sudan's paramilitary force, at war with the army since April 2023. It is accused of grave atrocities in Darfur.
Sumoud
A civilian political coalition led by former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, which calls for an end to the war and for civilian rule.

h: F.S. Aijazuddin: the grenade's pin has been pulled
dek: In Dawn, F.S. Aijazuddin surveys the chaos around the world and calls the new defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan a dangerous turn.
body: Pakistani writer and columnist F.S. Aijazuddin begins with Mao's saying that everything under heaven is in utter chaos. In his view, apart from China, leaders on no continent seem to be in control. In France, school students too young to vote are on the streets against crowded classrooms and a shortage of teachers, and in Ukraine Zelensky is caught between Putin on one side and Trump on the other.

According to the writer, the war of the United States and Israel with Iran has taken a dangerous turn. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have signed a defence pact, which he describes as a mix of Saudi money, Turkish weapons and Pakistani soldiers. He also points to a basic weakness: the three countries do not even share borders.

The pact copies NATO's Article 5, under which an attack on one is treated as an attack on all. Turkey is a NATO member, so in theory this circle reaches Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Aijazuddin notes that all three countries have Sunni majorities and all three governments do not tolerate dissent at home.

On Pakistan he writes that a leader and members of his party are in jail with no hope of pardon, and the centre is in conflict with the smaller provinces. The emergency and governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is an example. Drawing on lines by Khalil Gibran, he laments a nation divided into fragments, each fragment thinking itself a nation.

Finally the writer advises leaders to read Gibbon's history of the decline and fall of the Roman Empire and Marcus Aurelius's 'Meditations'. His conclusion is frightening: the grenade's pin has been pulled, and a doomsday blast is now only a matter of time.
nazar: Aijazuddin's warning matters because it is a Pakistani voice questioning his own country's new military alliance. Military alliances built on religious identity often open new fronts rather than bring peace, and ordinary soldiers and citizens pay the price. That Pakistan is being drawn into the Gulf war is a warning bell for South Asia, and it is also time for India to think about what role it can play in lowering tension in the region.
sawal: Can a military alliance built on religious identity bring peace?
ref: NATO's Article 5
The clause of the NATO treaty under which an attack on any one member is treated as an attack on all members.
Governor's rule
In Pakistan, during a constitutional emergency, the running of a province is taken from the elected government and handed to a governor appointed by the centre.

h: Child marriage in Bangladesh: close the gaps in the law
dek: According to an editorial in The Daily Star, the law to stop child marriage is still failing after nine years, because it has loopholes and enforcement is weak.
body: An editorial in the Bangladeshi newspaper The Daily Star says that almost ten years after the Child Marriage Restraint Act, 2017, lakhs of girls are still married before 18, which cannot be accepted. According to a recent review by UNICEF and UNFPA, 47.2 per cent of girls were married before 18 in 2025, compared with 51.4 per cent in 2019.

According to the paper, the biggest flaw is Section 19 of the law, which allows the marriage of a minor with court approval in 'special circumstances'. These circumstances are not defined anywhere, so the clause is easy to misuse, and the editorial demands that it be removed. A second problem is that the law punishes those who arrange the marriage but does not declare the marriage itself void, and under personal laws it remains valid.

The review recommends that children get the right to have their marriage annulled, that this law override conflicting personal laws, that the minimum age of marriage be 18 for both boys and girls, and that children caught in marriages face no criminal punishment.

On enforcement too things are bad. Prevention committees often do not work, officials lack training and resources, and the administration often arrives after the wedding has taken place. Families get fake birth certificates made or hold the wedding in a neighbouring district. At the root are poverty, few chances for education, insecurity and deep-rooted gender customs.

The editorial asks the government to have the Ministry of Women and Children Affairs lead legal reform, to place trained officials down to the union (local council) level, to register every marriage, and to provide rescue, treatment, safe shelter, counselling, legal aid and jobs for victims at state expense.
nazar: This is not just Bangladesh's story. In India too, despite the child marriage law, the practice continues in many areas, and here too the real question is poverty, girls' education and safety. The best thing about the editorial is that it stresses the rehabilitation and rights of the girls affected rather than punishment. Until a girl has school, work and the confidence to say 'no', the law will stay on paper.
sawal: Is giving girls opportunities more important than punishment?
ref: Child Marriage Restraint Act, 2017
Bangladesh's law that sets the minimum age at 18 for girls and 21 for boys, but allows an exception in 'special circumstances'.
UNFPA
The United Nations Population Fund, which works on reproductive health, gender equality and population issues.

h: Sumant Roy: e-waste is counted, the workers who handle it are not
dek: In The Wire, Sumant Roy writes that India has learned to count tonnes and certificates, but there is no account anywhere of the workers who sort, break down and repair e-waste.
body: 14 October is International E-Waste Day, and this year's theme is 'fast tech': cheap things thrown away quickly, such as earphones, charging cables, LED lights and electric toys. In Seelampur and Mustafabad in north-east Delhi, workers break up phones and TVs, sort scrap and extract copper in dangerous conditions, and many repair old goods to extend their life.

According to the writer, a reply in Parliament said India produced about 13.98 lakh tonnes of e-waste in 2024-25, of which 70.71 per cent was collected, recycled or disposed of. But in 2024 the government admitted in the Rajya Sabha that it has no estimate of how much e-waste the informal sector handles. The recycling percentage does not tell how many workers did the work, what they got, and in what conditions.

Under the E-Waste Rules, 2022, companies meet their 'extended producer responsibility' by buying certificates from registered recyclers. The Central Pollution Control Board set a minimum price of 22 rupees a kilo for these certificates, which Samsung and LG challenged in court. The writer argues that this fight is about companies' compliance costs, not wages. A costlier certificate does not by itself improve a waste picker's earnings or safety.

Roy does not argue for keeping dangerous recycling alive in the name of livelihood. He suggests that part of the producer responsibility money be set aside for safe workplaces, medical care and training, that waste pickers' cooperatives become direct partners, like Pune's 'SWaCH' cooperative, and that a right-to-repair law be made under which spare parts and information are easy to get.
The writer's conclusion is that recognising workers means fair pay, protection and a voice in the system. Fast tech is fast because someone else is paying its slow cost.
nazar: This piece brings out the face of the 'clean' and 'green' economy that numbers hide. Most workers in Seelampur and Mustafabad are poor, migrant and often from minorities, and their lungs pay the price of the phones we keep changing. Until environmental policy includes the health and pay of workers, even high recycling percentages will remain only half the truth.
sawal: Who is paying the real price of the phones we throw away?
ref: Extended producer responsibility (EPR)
A rule under which companies making electrical goods must take responsibility for collecting and recycling the waste from their products.
Right to repair
The right of consumers and independent repairers to get spare parts, tools and information, so goods can be fixed instead of thrown away.

h: Krishnan Srinivasan: weak and broke, but the United Nations is still alive
dek: In The Wire, former foreign secretary Krishnan Srinivasan argues that despite all of Trump's attacks, the need for the United Nations has not ended, especially on questions like AI.
body: On 22 September, at the UN General Assembly, Donald Trump declared that multilateralism is dead and the world should accept American leadership. India's former foreign secretary Krishnan Srinivasan calls these claims exaggerated and in places wrong.

According to the writer, the picture in 2026 is the opposite: the Russia-Ukraine war is heading into its fifth year, there has been no reckoning for the atrocities in Gaza, settlements are spreading in the West Bank and Israel has reached close to Beirut in Lebanon. Yet at the very time Trump was threatening Iran with destruction, American and Iranian representatives were talking for hours behind closed doors about ending the war. In the writer's eyes this is the UN's real value: a forum that brings 193 countries to one place, where difficult talks become possible.

The money crisis is deep. The United States cut voluntary contributions and delayed required payments, though just before the General Assembly debate it paid 725 million dollars of regular dues and 102 million dollars for peacekeeping, which kept its vote safe. The writer concludes that for now the Trump administration does not see the collapse of the institution as being in its interest.

This contradiction is clearest on artificial intelligence (AI). Trump rejected international rules for AI safety as a 'globalist plot', while the leaders of Finland and Norway launched an appeal to keep powerful AI models under human oversight, which 20 countries have joined. At the Security Council, the heads of OpenAI and Anthropic argued for international standards.

Srinivasan believes the UN's strength lies not in binding decisions but in identifying shared problems, shaping rules and building coalitions before consensus. It is already weak, poor and divided, but reports of its death are premature.
nazar: For the Global South a forum like the UN matters because every country there has one vote, however small it is. In an age of powerful countries doing as they please, if this forum weakens, poor countries will lose the most. The writer's faith seems a little too hopeful, because from Gaza to Ukraine the UN has failed to stop atrocities. Still, the alternative is the law of might, which serves no one.
sawal: If the UN goes, where will the voice of weak countries go?
ref: Multilateralism
A system in which the world's problems are solved by many countries together through shared institutions and rules, not by one power alone.
UN General Assembly
The body of the United Nations in which all 193 member countries sit with equal votes.

h: Ten years since Najeeb: his mother still watches the door
dek: On the tenth anniversary of the disappearance of JNU student Najeeb Ahmed, student groups held a march and demanded accountability.
body: Fatima Nafees of Badaun still hopes her son will return. Maktoob's report says the family had thought of putting up a nameplate with all three sons' names on the house, so that if Najeeb came back he would recognise it. Najeeb Ahmed, a first-year MSc Biotechnology student, went missing from JNU on 15 October 2016. It is alleged that the night before, students linked to the ABVP beat him up in Mahi-Mandavi hostel.

Delhi Police, a special investigation team, the Crime Branch and then the CBI all investigated, but none could trace him. On Wednesday, the tenth anniversary, BAPSA, the Fraternity Movement and the Muslim Students Federation held a 'Justice for Najeeb' march on campus. Slogans were raised against the police, the CBI and Islamophobia, along with a demand for the release of Sharjeel Imam and Umar Khalid.

The organisers also pointed a finger at the Left-led students' union of the time. They allege that the union's office-bearers then signed letters to the warden that painted Najeeb as a culprit and mentally ill, and that this same story was later taken up by the administration, the police and the CBI. BAPSA-backed councillor Komal Devi tore up a letter at the march and said the case must be kept alive.
On Thursday AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi asked the central government to share any information it has about Najeeb, so that his mother can at least go there.
nazar: Four agencies in ten years could not trace one student. Whether that is failure or indifference is a question that still stands. Najeeb's case reminds us that without accountability, justice becomes nothing but waiting, and that waiting weighs heaviest on a mother's life.
sawal: A student has been missing for ten years. Who is accountable?
ref: Najeeb Ahmed
A JNU student who went missing in October 2016, the day after an alleged assault in his hostel. The CBI filed a report closing the investigation in 2018.
BAPSA
Birsa Ambedkar Phule Students' Association, an Ambedkarite student organisation at JNU.

h: Detained outside IIT after coming to seek justice for Sahil Wakode
dek: Mumbai Police detained Ambedkarite leaders who gathered on a 'Chalo IIT Bombay' call over the death of a Dalit student at IIT Bombay.
body: Sahil Wakode, a 22-year-old second-year BTech student at IIT Bombay, was found dead in his hostel room on the evening of 18 September. According to Maktoob's report, a police officer says he had been caught allegedly cheating in an exam, and had admitted the mistake in writing and asked for another chance.

On his father's complaint, Powai police have registered a case of abetment to suicide against Professor Doola. The professor denies the harassment allegations. The Mumbai Crime Branch has recorded statements from more than 40 people. Sahil's parents, Ravindra and Sonali Wakode, have been on hunger strike at Azad Maidan since 24 September and allege caste discrimination at the institute.

On Wednesday people gathered outside the campus on a 'Chalo IIT Bombay' (Let's go to IIT Bombay) call, but the police did not let the protest happen at all. There was heavy deployment around the campus, entry was barred, and several Ambedkarite leaders, including Rahul Sonpimple, Deepali Salve and Sambhaji Bhagat, were detained. There were reports that his father Ravindra Wakode was also detained, but the police denied this.
The protesters demand that responsibility for the death be fixed and that the allegations of caste discrimination be investigated fairly. The report records no response from the IIT administration.
nazar: From Rohith Vemula to Darshan Solanki, every time there is a death on campus, the first question is why the institution does not listen. When parents have been sitting hungry for three weeks and those seeking justice are stopped right at the gate, the complaint of discrimination only grows deeper.
sawal: When will our big campuses listen to Dalit students?
ref: Darshan Solanki
A Dalit student at IIT Bombay who died in February 2023. His family alleged caste discrimination.

h: Ankita Bhandari's parents detained at India Gate
dek: Security personnel removed the family and Congress MPs who were sitting in protest against the appointment as Sikkim governor of a BJP leader accused of being the 'VIP'.
body: According to Scroll's report, security personnel detained Ankita Bhandari's parents and Congress MPs who were protesting at India Gate. Citing ANI, it said the parents were released in less than two hours. The protest began after BJP leader Dushyant Kumar Gautam was made Governor of Sikkim on Monday. The family and activists allege that Gautam is the 'VIP' whose name has been linked to the murder.

Nineteen-year-old Ankita was a receptionist at a resort in Rishikesh owned by Pulkit Arya, son of former BJP leader Vinod Arya. She went missing in September 2022 and her body was found in the Chilla canal six days later. Pulkit and two associates were sentenced to life imprisonment in May 2025. Messages that came out later led to the allegation that she was pressured to give 'special services' to a VIP and was killed when she refused.

Gautam's name came up in alleged audio and video of former BJP MLA Suresh Rathore. Rathore denied them, yet he was arrested in June. The special investigation team reportedly found no evidence of any influential leader's role. Gautam denies the allegations and has filed a defamation suit in the Delhi High Court. In January Chief Minister Dhami had spoken of recommending a CBI probe.
The family has appealed to the President to put the appointment on hold until the CBI probe is complete, and for the probe to focus on the VIP angle.
nazar: Giving a constitutional post to a man facing allegations in a case still under investigation, and then removing grieving parents from their protest, together send one message. Seeking justice cannot be a crime.
sawal: Why the governor's post before the investigation is complete?
ref: Ankita Bhandari murder
The murder of a receptionist at a resort in Rishikesh in September 2022. The resort owner and two employees were given life sentences.

h: Custodial death in Bettiah, six policemen suspended
dek: Police say Dilshad Ansari jumped from a moving vehicle; his family alleges he was beaten.
body: Six policemen, including two sub-inspectors, have been suspended after the death of 25-year-old Dilshad Ansari in police custody in West Champaran, Bihar. According to SabrangIndia's report, Dilshad was an accused in an NDPS case from August 2025. He leaves behind his wife Naghma Khatoon and a six-month-old daughter.

His wife says the police took him from home at about two in the morning on 12 October and said they would let him go by morning after questioning. Later a call came from the police station saying his health had worsened. When the family reached GMCH Bettiah, doctors said he had been brought dead.

A statement from Bettiah police said that while being taken into custody Dilshad jumped from the moving vehicle and was badly injured. The family does not accept this. His father Akhbar Ansari alleges that his son was hit hard on the head. Ali Anwar, head of the Pasmanda Muslim Mahaz and a former Rajya Sabha MP, asked why, if someone jumped, there were no injuries on his hands and legs. He demanded action from the Chief Minister, intervention by the National Human Rights Commission and compensation for the family.
The family wants a high-level inquiry, and on social media there are demands for a fair investigation based on CCTV footage and the post-mortem report.
nazar: Suspension is a first step, not justice. In every custodial death, stories like 'he jumped from the vehicle' or 'he fell ill' are repeated, and most cases get buried in files. Without an independent inquiry and a public post-mortem, trust will not return.
sawal: Why are the stories of custodial deaths the same every time?
ref: NDPS Act
The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985. A strict law on drug-related offences.

h: Dalit woman alleges she was beaten for drawing water from a well
dek: On Manju Chaudhary's complaint in Jagannathpur, Ranchi, an FIR has been filed against five people under the SC/ST Act.
body: In Sector 2 of HEC Smart City in Ranchi, the capital of Jharkhand, a Dalit woman has alleged that neighbours beat her and hurled casteist abuse at her over drawing water from a well. According to The Mooknayak's report, the case falls under Jagannathpur police station.

According to Manju Chaudhary's complaint, five people living near her house had been stopping her from drawing water from the well since 23 July. On 10 October, it is alleged, they suddenly attacked her badly and humiliated her over her caste. She went to the police station the same day. According to the police, the well is inside the compound of the main accused's house.

The complaint names Amrendra Kumar, his wife Remi Devi, their two sons and one other person. The police have filed an FIR under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act and sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Station in-charge Nitin Kumar Singh said all the allegations are being investigated and legal action will follow.
On Monday the accused family also filed a counter-complaint, accusing the woman herself of assault.
nazar: The Chavdar Tank satyagraha at Mahad is nearly a hundred years old, yet access to water is still a fight for Dalits, and that too in a 'smart city'. Counter-complaints are common in such cases, so the investigation must be quick and fair.
sawal: Why does caste still guard water, even in a smart city?
ref: Mahad Satyagraha
The 1927 movement led by Dr Ambedkar for the right of Dalits to take water from the Chavdar Tank at Mahad.

h: Super El Nino looms, Zimbabwe stocks grain for drought
dek: Zimbabwe is building a 500 million dollar reserve of cash and grain, because a severe drought is feared in the coming rainy season.
body: According to Down To Earth's report, Zimbabwe's Finance Minister Mthuli Ncube announced a 500 million dollar reserve of cash and grain on 14 October. The country's weather service estimates an 88 to 94 per cent chance of a super El Nino forming in the 2026-27 rainy season. The Columbia Climate School's forecast also points to below-average rain from September to November and a deepening drought in December and January.

In September the cabinet approved a six-part plan: grain reserves, climate-smart farming, farm loans, protection of livestock, grain imports and early warning systems. 'Pfumvudza' conservation farming, with small, carefully tended plots, is being expanded, and farmers are being told to grow traditional drought-hardy grains like sorghum and millet.

The biggest worry is cattle. The agriculture ministry estimates that 22.3 lakh cattle will be at risk in the 2027-28 lean season. Feeding them will need 4.05 lakh tonnes of fodder, while a shortfall of 2.33 lakh tonnes is feared. Wheat farmers have been told not to burn stalks but to save them for fodder.
The report says rural families who depend on rain are most at risk, and the plan's success depends on how quickly and on how large a scale it reaches the ground.
nazar: El Nino also affects India's monsoon, and this year Maharashtra is already struggling with drought. Zimbabwe is storing grain and fodder in advance, and that is a lesson for us too: preparing before a drought is better than handing out relief after it comes.
sawal: Are we preparing for the next drought in advance?
ref: El Nino
An unusual warming of the Pacific Ocean's waters that upsets rainfall patterns around the world. It often brings drought to southern Africa and India.

h: How many villages will Polavaram's water drown? No one knows for sure
dek: Adivasi villages in the Konta area of Sukma live in fear of being submerged by Andhra Pradesh's Polavaram project, but the count of affected villages in government papers changes every time.
body: Konta in Chhattisgarh's Sukma district lies on the banks of the Sabari river, a tributary of the Godavari. Manglu Dorla's family has farmed here for generations and depends on the forest for fuel, fodder and food. Mongabay India's report says people here do not know whether water from the Polavaram irrigation project being built in Andhra Pradesh will reach their homes, or whom to ask.

The reason is that government figures do not match. A 2006 report said four villages and about 11,766 people in Chhattisgarh would be affected. In 2013 the Centre told Parliament eight villages; in 2020 the state Assembly was told nine villages and about 18,510 people. A CAG audit presented in March 2026 counts 12 villages in Chhattisgarh and Odisha, while the Bastariya Raj Morcha says 18 villages could be submerged. On a visit to Sukma on 28 September, Chief Minister Vishnu Deo Sai admitted the count could go above 18. The report of the survey that was spoken of in 2022 has still not been made public.

According to the report, to protect against flooding, about 29 kilometres of embankments were to be built along the Sabari in Chhattisgarh and 30 kilometres in Odisha. The CAG found that work on them had not even begun. In 2009 an Environment Ministry committee directed public hearings in both states, which never happened. A stop-work order came in 2011, but it stayed in cold storage for more than ten years and construction went on. Now Andhra Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu has promised to complete the project by 2027.

Local former MLA Manish Kunjam says it is not just the homes of the Koya and Dorla Adivasis but their culture and traditions that are at stake. According to Himanshu Thakkar, who works on rivers, the Forest Rights Act has been violated and the effect of the backwater was never assessed. The district collector said the matter does not fall under his department.

The Bastariya Raj Morcha demands that the survey be made public, the names of those affected be disclosed, compensation be paid before displacement, and schooling in the local language and jobs be arranged at resettlement sites.
nazar: In the story of big dams, the first to disappear are the ones who drown first. When even after twenty years it is not settled how many Adivasi villages will go under, this should be seen not as carelessness but as a way of keeping these people out of the count. Not a single village should be submerged without a public hearing and the consent of the gram sabha (village assembly).
sawal: Why are the people whose village will drown the last to be told?
ref: Polavaram project
A multipurpose dam on the Godavari in Andhra Pradesh, declared a national project in 2014. Its submergence area reaches Adivasi areas of Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
Koya and Dorla
Adivasi communities of Bastar and the Godavari valley, whose lives depend on farming, the forest and the river.

h: A hospital in Mahoba waiting three years for a doctor
dek: Tindauhi village in Mahoba has an Ayurvedic hospital, but villagers say no regular doctor has sat there for years.
body: Tindauhi village in the Kabrai block of Uttar Pradesh's Mahoba district has an Ayurvedic hospital, but for the villagers it has become just a building. According to Khabar Lahariya's report, people say that for about three years no doctor has come there regularly.

Villagers say that with no doctor, they have to go to private hospitals even for minor illnesses, where the cost of treatment weighs heavily on their pockets. In this part of Bundelkhand, where households run on farming and daily wage work, this cost hits their livelihood directly.
The district Ayurvedic officer blames a shortage of doctors. He claims doctors do go there on fixed days. The villagers' experience does not match this, and the report puts this gap in front of us.
nazar: Village health often rests on hospitals like this, whose walls are counted in government figures but whose doctors are not. It is local journalism like Khabar Lahariya's that turns such empty rooms into news, which would otherwise be recorded nowhere.
sawal: What use is a hospital without a doctor?
ref: Khabar Lahariya
A news organisation run by rural women that began in Bundelkhand and reports from small towns and villages.

h: Delhi in the world's eyes: 'the shell of democracy stands, something inside is rotting'
dek: The American independent broadcaster Democracy Now! spoke at length with The Wire's Jahnavi Sen and Scroll's Shoaib Daniyal about the movement against names being cut from the voter rolls and the mass arrests in Delhi.
body: The New York-based independent news programme Democracy Now! gave about fifteen minutes to India in its 12 October episode. Hosts Amy Goodman and Anjali Kamat called it the biggest challenge in the Modi government's twelve years: a movement against the removal of about 130 million names from the voter rolls, which protesters are calling 'vote theft'. Their demand is that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign and that the election system be fundamentally reformed.

According to the programme, the movement is led by the student and youth 'Cockroach' movement, whose name comes from a remark earlier this year in which the Chief Justice of India compared unemployed young people to cockroaches. Opposition parties joined later. In a clip, Rahul Gandhi says the government shut down the city with thousands of police, when all the opposition wants is for the government to prove the election was not rigged.

Goodman says that before Saturday's protest, trains were cancelled in Delhi, metro stations were shut and mobile internet was blocked across large areas. According to her, at least seven thousand people were detained on Saturday alone, including movement leaders, lawyers and journalists. When the UN human rights spokesperson expressed concern, the Indian mission in Geneva dismissed it as unwarranted interference.

Scroll's political editor Shoaib Daniyal was himself arrested on Saturday. He says the process of cutting names was arbitrary and hit Muslims far harder than other citizens. He calls it a Gen Z movement and says the right to vote is the foundation of all other rights. He also faults the Supreme Court, which in his view held hearings while names were being cut but stopped nothing.

The Wire's managing editor Jahnavi Sen says opposition leaders had first tried to meet the Election Commission and the President, and then wanted to give a memorandum to the Chief Justice. When the meeting was refused, it turned into a big march. She alleges that the police detained women without women constables and after dark, which is against the law, that people were driven around in buses for hours and dropped in far corners of the city, and that they were pressured to delete videos.

According to Sen, journalists wearing press cards were also picked up, and CPI(M) MP John Brittas was crushed in a bus so badly that he had to be taken to hospital. On Sunday the Supreme Court ordered a halt to illegal detentions, but in her view nothing changed on the ground. The conversation ends on Daniyal's point that the outer shell of democracy in India still stands, but something inside has rotted.
nazar: This is not a crafted documentary but a report straight from the street, and its value is that the world is hearing what is happening in Delhi in the words of an Indian journalist, not in an official statement. It is easy to invoke the 'largest democracy' in Geneva, but the real test of democracy is whose name was cut from the voter roll and what the police did to those asking questions.
When the court gives an order and the detentions still do not stop, the matter is no longer just about one movement; it becomes about the credibility of institutions.
sawal: If your name is not on the list, are you still a citizen?
ref: Democracy Now!
An independent, ad-free daily news programme running from New York since 1996. Amy Goodman is its founding host, and it is known for coverage of war, human rights and movements.
Voter roll revision

The Election Commission checks the voter rolls from time to time and removes dead, duplicate or shifted names. Critics allege that this time the process also cut the names of legitimate citizens in large numbers.

h: A hundred rupees, borrowed chairs and Premchand's tonga
dek: On Samalochan, Sajjad Zaheer's full memoir telling the inside story of the preparations for the first Progressive Writers' conference in 1936.
body: To mark ninety years of the Progressive Writers' Association, Samalochan has published a long Urdu essay by Sajjad Zaheer in Hindi. It appeared in 1956 in his book Roshnai (Ink). According to the editorial note, only a cut-down version was available in Hindi until now; this is the full text. The translation is by Tanveer Hasan, and the original text was gathered by Manoj Mohan.

The essay opens with light satire. Zaheer says we hold so many gatherings that a class of professional organisers has grown up who know all about tents, electricity and donations. Rich organisations' gatherings leave behind quarrels over donations, and poor organisations' organisers sink into debt. The progressive writers did not even have this skill.

The conference was set for April 1936 in Lucknow, around the time of the Congress session, so that Left and progressive people would be in the city anyway. Several names were considered for president, and in the end Premchand agreed. The budget was a hundred to a hundred and twenty-five rupees, and not even the hall was fixed. Later the Rifah-e-Aam Hall was given free, chairs were borrowed, and Rashid Jahan and her companions sold tickets.

Along with literature, the agenda took in the world: colonial curbs on expression, Italy's attack on Ethiopia, Japan in China and the rise of fascism in Europe. Zaheer also worries about the growing distance between Hindi and Urdu.

The most memorable picture is of Premchand, who arrived by tonga (horse cart) straight at the house with no welcome at all. The writer pauses on his simplicity. The text breaks off as Maulana Hasrat Mohani arrives, meaning the next part is still to come.
nazar: Today, when writers' bodies have either melted into government events or split into rival camps, this essay reminds us that a great movement began with empty pockets, borrowed chairs and a shared concern. Fascism, freedom of expression and the distance between Hindi and Urdu: ninety years later these questions still stand just as they did.
sawal: On what shared question would today's writers gather in one hall?
ref: Progressive Writers' Association
A writers' body formed in Lucknow in 1936, whose first session was chaired by Premchand. Its aim was to link literature with society and the freedom struggle.
Sajjad Zaheer
Urdu writer and one of the founders of the Association (1905-1973). The collection Angarey (Embers) and Roshnai (Ink) are his best-known books.

h: Curfew, a broken tank and a kite flying across the border
dek: On Sammukh, five poems by Odia poet Shakti Mahanti, in Gargi Mishra's Hindi translation, that look at home and child in the midst of violence.
body: Sammukh has published five poems by Odia poet Shakti Mahanti under the title Curfew ki Khabar aur Anya Kavitayen (News of Curfew and Other Poems). The translation is by Gargi Mishra, a young poet and sociology researcher. The introduction describes the poems as emotionally sharp and unwilling to look away from their time. We are not reproducing the poems here; read them on the original page.

The first poem is set in a city under curfew, where a woman who speaks up for girls' education is shot. The poet links the attack to the fear of a woman's freedom and the wish to control her body, and also sees in it the silent complicity of the police, the self-appointed guardians of religion and ordinary men.
The second poem is a morning after a war has ended. Families are still in mourning, children play near a wrecked tank, grass sprouts from sandbags, and at the end a kite drifts across the border.

Two poems are set inside the home. In one, a father answers his son's questions about the sunset, eclipses and dying stars, and silently wishes that his son be spared his burden. In the other, a little girl questions her father, who raises his hand against her mother, and wings and sky become her dream of escape.
The last poem is about a poet whose inner spring has dried up and who sits down to write a novel, but cannot let go of his bond with poetry.
nazar: Hindi readers have few ways to reach contemporary poetry in other Indian languages, so translations like these are precious. In these poems public violence and domestic violence are bound in a single thread, and that is their strength.
sawal: Is curfew imposed on the city, or inside the home?
ref: Shakti Mahanti
A contemporary poet writing in Odia. According to Sammukh's introduction, his poetry confronts its time head-on.
photo_note: Akash ke Siddh (Siddhas of the sky)

h: Julia's death, a tale of a jinn, and a woman who writes
dek: On Sammukh, Neha Naruka's satirical prose uses a superstitious tale spun around a girl's death to question the lives of women.
body: This instalment of Neha Naruka's series Mritatmaon ka Desh (Land of the Dead Souls) is titled Julia aur Jinn ka Chakkar (Julia and the Jinn Business). The poet herself says the subject of her series is death, so she does not name living Hindi writers. Right at the start she takes a dig at the literary world: when she asked a writer for the secret of writing, she got a comment on her clothes instead, and editors who lecture on 'boldness' have put her off the very word.
She says the books of a woman novelist once filled her with restlessness. She could not make a revolution, so she began writing poetry and became one more name in the crowd of poets.

Then comes the story of Julia, with the name changed: a girl studying for her BA who swam like a fish in water. Years later, at a wedding, her mother met the writer and said Julia was no more, and then kept laughing for a long time. Her friends said a jinn from a tree had come home with her, and it was the jinn that finally took her life. There is also talk of burning in this tale.

The writer leaves it to the reader to believe the tale or not, but she also raises a sharp question: how hard it is for a woman travelling just to reach a toilet. She shares her experiences of travelling by bus and on highways, and says with a laugh that she never met any jinn.
The whole piece moves in a light tone, but beneath it lie layers of a woman's body, fear and silence.
nazar: Putting a girl's suspicious death down to a jinn or a ghost is an old habit of our society, one that buries the real questions. Neha Naruka's satire pricks a needle into this silence. A woman reader rightly wrote in a comment that a woman's life is like dying a little every day.
sawal: What question does the tale of the jinn really cover up?
ref: Neha Naruka
Hindi poet. She received the 2024 Vagishwari Samman for her poetry collection Phati Hatheliyan (Cracked Palms).

h: Natsamrat's cry: when the line between stage and life disappears
dek: On Hindwi's Bela, Naveen Rangiyal's essay reads the loneliness and grief of the artist through Nana Patekar's Ganpatrao Belwalkar.
body: Naveen Rangiyal's essay is not a review but a viewer's confession. Its subject is Ganpatrao Ramchandra Belwalkar, the character Nana Patekar plays in the Marathi film Natsamrat (The Emperor of Actors): an old actor who steps off the stage and becomes homeless in life.

The writer's opening argument is that an artist who lives by erasing the line between truth and dream has no fixed home; he stays displaced both inside and outside. In the film, Ganpatrao's cry as he begs for a home in a dark lane seems to him the very limit of grief.

He says he watched the film in a neglected cinema hall in Maharashtra. He did not fully understand Marathi, yet the film took him where even his mother tongue could not, and he felt that he and Ganpatrao were the same man.

The essay places this character in the line of Shakespeare's Hamlet, Lear, Othello and Julius Caesar, and goes on to Beckett. The writer also mentions Nana Patekar's characters in Wajood and Prahaar, who have a broken heart inside a hard outer shell.

He recalls that the original play is by Kusumagraj, that is V.V. Shirwadkar, and says Nana Patekar made this character immortal on screen. The Marathi line in the title says just this: there will never be another Natsamrat like him.
nazar: Ageing parents becoming strangers in their own home is what makes Natsamrat bigger than the story of one actor. This essay shows that good acting crosses the wall of language, and more such bridges should be built between Hindi and Marathi.
sawal: What is the last stage for an ageing artist?
ref: Natsamrat
Kusumagraj's (V.V. Shirwadkar's) 1970 Marathi play, thought to be inspired by King Lear. A film starring Nana Patekar was made in 2016.
Kusumagraj
A major Marathi poet and playwright (1912-1999). He received the Jnanpith Award.

h: An irritated satire on popcorn crunching in the cinema
dek: On Hindwi's Bela, Kumar Keshav's satire uses the noise of popcorn chewing to talk about attention in the cinema and the rights of others.
body: Kumar Keshav's satire begins with a familiar irritation: the most serious scene of the film is playing, and from the next seat comes the sound of popcorn being chewed. The writer jokingly calls it 'cinematic terrorism'.

He records every sound, from the tub being opened and a hand going in, to groping for a kernel and chewing it, and names the tub as a partner in this crime. He gives an example too: if this sound comes during a silent scene with news of a father's death, all the viewer's feeling falls apart.

According to the writer, the habit started in America in the 1930s, when cinema owners let in the cheap popcorn sold outside. About today's multiplexes he asks why popcorn must be sold with every film, and why the cinema hall has become a food court.

He says he has nothing against eating popcorn, but other viewers have rights too. In this age split between phones, notifications and reels, the cinema is one of the few places where you can cut yourself off from the world in darkness and silence.

Along the way, he gets laughs by imagining famous scenes from Sholay, Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge, Lagaan and Drishyam amid the crunching. At the end the satire widens, as he demands a special session of Parliament and a high-level committee on the problem.
nazar: This light-looking piece is really about the shared manners of public spaces, which are slowly disappearing. It is also about how the multiplex business now rests more on expensive food counters than on films.
sawal: Who is the keeper of the silence in a dark cinema hall?
ref: Bela

h: Is asking a poet about his job an insult or a fair question?
dek: On Hindwi's Bela, Lalan Chaturvedi's satire, in which a self-admiring poet's visit leaves behind a question about poetry and livelihood.
body: In Lalan Chaturvedi's satire, the poet Pyarelal turns up unannounced at the narrator's house. The narrator is not pleased; a married man has his own busy life. Pyarelal is unmarried, and poetry is his only beloved.

His dream is a 'poetry palace' with poems written in golden letters on its walls, and for this he talks of a public-private partnership model. He is ready to recite poetry at every chance. Here the writer takes a dig at today's poet: the old poet was a carefree wanderer, the new poet is smart and instant.

The story turns over tea. The narrator's wife has heard from someone that being a poet's wife is bad luck. She brings tea and asks straight out whether, apart from poetry, the poet has any work, business or job. The poet gets up hurt, and the narrator is embarrassed.

On his way out the poet tells the story of a folk artist, 'Kapichhavi', who imitated all kinds of figures. When his admirers dwindled, he began performing at rich people's wedding processions, and one day, broken by someone's insult, he left the area altogether. In the poet's eyes, asking an artist about his job is the same kind of insult.
The satire strikes both ways: at the poet's self-admiration, and at society's way of looking at an artist that weighs him only by what he earns.
nazar: Most writers in Hindi cannot run a home on poetry, and the question of what a writer should live on is the real gap in our cultural set-up. This satire makes us laugh, but the wife's question does not seem unfair, and Kapichhavi's story is not false either.
sawal: Should an artist be respected for his work or for his earnings?
ref: Bahurupiya tradition
Folk artists who take on many different guises and perform in villages and towns. With patronage shrinking, this tradition is now close to dying out.
